samples.summary: The new URL gate is bypassable: `escapeMarkdownText` leaves `(` and `)` unescaped, so an attacker-controlled text run adjacent to the unescaped `[image]` / `[nested table]` placeholders forms a live Markdown link with an arbitrary (e.g. `javascript:`) destination in the exported `.md`.
samples.evidence:
`escapeMarkdownText` (markdown.ts:479-482) escapes `\ * _ [ ] ` ~ <` but NOT `(` or `)`. That is safe for a normal run, because every literal `[`/`]` in run text is escaped — but two code paths emit *unescaped* brackets: `imageInline` returns the literal `'[image]'` (markdown.ts:423 and :430) and `cellToMarkdown` pushes `'[nested table]'` (markdown.ts:175). `inlinesToMarkdown` concatenates runs with no separator (markdown.ts:190-196).

Attack: a hostile collaborator's CRDT write (or a crafted `.docx`/HTML paste — the exact provenance the gate's own docstring names at markdown.ts:249-251) puts two inlines in one paragraph:
  1. `{ style: { image: { src: 'javascript:x', ... } } }` → `isSafeImageSrc` rejects it → the gate emits `[image]`;
  2. `{ text: '(javascript:alert(1))' }` → escaped to `(javascript:alert(1))` unchanged.
The serializer emits `[image](javascript:alert(1))` — a syntactically valid CommonMark inline link whose destination is exactly the scheme `isEmittableUrl` exists to keep out. With `inlineImages:false` (the CLI default) *any* `data:` src reaches the placeholder, so no unsafe src is even required. The same works with the `[nested table]` placeholder inside a GFM cell (`|` is escaped there, parentheses are not).

A second spelling: if the image is the first inline of a block and the next run begins `: javascript:alert(1)`, the emitted line is `[image]: javascript:alert(1)`, a CommonMark **link reference definition** that makes every later `[image]` in the file a `javascript:` link.

This defeats the stated goal of the change ("the produced `.md` is opened by a renderer that will happily make `javascript:` or `data:text/html` clickable", markdown.ts:219-223) and of the CLI test that asserts `expect(cap.stdout).not.toContain('](')` for a dropped href (packages/cli/test/docs-content.test.ts:167). No test in `packages/docs/test/serialize/markdown.test.ts` places attacker text immediately after a placeholder. Fix: escape `(`/`)` in run text, or emit the placeholder with its brackets escaped (`\[image\]`).

samples.summary: PDF export validates the WHATWG-normalized form of `style.href` and then writes the raw string into the `/URI` action — an acknowledged parser differential shipped rather than fixed ("issue #988 … deliberately left out of this change").
samples.evidence: `isSafeUrl(style.href)` runs `new URL(href)` (packages/core/src/url/index.ts:24-31), which deletes every tab/LF/CR and trims leading/trailing C0-or-space before reading the scheme; `addLinkAnnotation(page, rect, style.href)` at pdf-painter.ts:856 then writes the *unvalidated raw* string. Validated-string ≠ emitted-string is the same defect class the Markdown gate in this very diff was rewritten three times to close (see `UNEMITTABLE_URL_CHARS`, markdown.ts:263). I could not construct a raw string that a PDF viewer resolves to an unsafe scheme while `new URL()` reports a safe one (the parser trims/deletes rather than inserts), so I could not complete the exploit chain — but the invariant is broken and the fix is one line (`addLinkAnnotation(..., new URL(style.href).href)` or a literal-character gate). Shipping a known-broken security gate behind an issue number leaves it reading as covered.

samples.summary: `resolvePageSetup`'s hardening against hostile geometry has no lower or upper bound on the paper dimensions — only `Number.isFinite && > 0` — so a collaborator's CRDT write or an imported `.docx` can still store a sub-pixel or astronomically large page that every replica must lay out.
samples.evidence:
`usableSize` (types.ts:766-770) accepts any finite positive number, and `MIN_CONTENT_PX` is applied only to the *margin* fit (`fitMargins`, types.ts:784-798), never to `paperSize.width/height`. The change's own test pins a 0.5 px page as acceptable (packages/docs/test/model/types.test.ts, 'never produces a NaN margin on a page smaller than the content floor'), while `MIN_CONTENT_PX`'s docstring states 1 px is what `paginateLayout` needs to make progress — so the resolver knowingly returns boxes below its own stated floor.

Vector: a hostile collaborator writes `pageSetup.paperSize = { width: 0.5, height: 0.5 }` (or `parsePageSetup` yields 1 px from `<w:pgSz w:w="15"/>`, since `sectPrLengthPx` only requires `> 0`). `resolvePageSetup` clamps margins to 0 and returns a 0.5×0.5 content box; `paginateLayout` (pagination.ts:55-56, 91) then starts a new page per line, so an N-character document becomes ~N pages, each rendered as its own canvas sheet — CPU/memory exhaustion on every replica that opens the document, with no local write ever having validated it. The symmetric case (`width: 1e20` from `<w:pgSz w:w="99999999999"/>`) yields a page no canvas can allocate. Since this function is explicitly the boundary for "data we do not control", a `[MIN_PAGE_PX, MAX_PAGE_PX]` clamp belongs here alongside the NaN/negative handling.

samples.summary: `safeFilename`, now extended to the two new `.md`/`.txt` export paths, strips only `\ / : * ? " < > |` — it leaves C0 control characters, RTL/bidi overrides and a leading dot in the attacker-influenceable document title.
samples.evidence: The title reaches `safeFilename` from the document name, which a collaborator can set. `(title || "").replace(/[\\/:*?"<>|]+/g, "_")` (export-utils.ts:110) passes through U+202E (RIGHT-TO-LEFT OVERRIDE), so a title like `report‮dm.txt` renders in the download shelf and file manager as a different-looking extension, and control characters survive into the suggested filename. The two new entries in `docs-export-button.tsx` route through the same helper. Pre-existing (identical for the already-shipped `.pdf`/`.docx`) and browsers do additional sanitising of `a.download`, hence nit — but the change widens the extension union without touching the sanitiser.

verdict.reason: Verified directly in the repo. escapeMarkdownText (packages/docs/src/serialize/markdown.ts:478-482) escapes only \ * _ [ ] ` ~ < — not '(' , ')' or ':'. Two paths emit UNESCAPED brackets: imageInline returns the literal '[image]' at markdown.ts:423 (data: src with inlineImages off, the CLI default) and markdown.ts:430 (isSafeImageSrc rejection), and cellToMarkdown pushes literal '[nested table]' at markdown.ts:175 (only '|' escaped, markdown.ts:181). inlinesToMarkdown concatenates runs with no separator (markdown.ts:190-196) and blockToMarkdown returns paragraph text verbatim (markdown.ts:112-113). Therefore an image inline whose src is rejected by the gate, followed by a text run '(javascript:alert(1))', serializes to '[image](javascript:alert(1))' — a valid CommonMark inline link (balanced parens in the destination) carrying exactly the scheme isEmittableUrl/isSafeImageSrc (markdown.ts:384-410) exist to block; escapeMarkdownHref (markdown.ts:515-517) never runs on this path. Since ':' is also unescaped, the '[image]: javascript:...' link-reference-definition variant holds too. The threat model is the code's own docstrings (markdown.ts:219-223, 249-251: HTML paste / DOCX import / collaborator CRDT write, renderer makes javascript: clickable), and the CLI asserts the opposite invariant (packages/cli/test/docs-content.test.ts:172-173, 220). No test in packages/docs/test/serialize/markdown.test.ts (256, 343-398, 637-794) places text adjacent to a placeholder, and I found no upstream sanitizer or guard that escapes/separates the placeholders. Bypassable URL/protocol gate = in-lane injection/auth-of-content weakness; not refutable.
